stem: The WHO definition of impairment is:

options.html: Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure/function
The inability of a person to perform at a satisfactory level in an activity in which they want to succeed
Any loss or abnormality of technical expertise previously possessed by an individual

answer: The correct answer is A. Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure/function. Contrast with disability in Q2 — impairment is just the lack of function.

stem: The WHO definition of disability is:

options.html: Any activity that creates an improvement in the ability of an individual to perform, accomplish, or complete an activity in the manner beyond their baseline performance
Any activity limitation that creates a difficulty in the performance, accomplishment, or completion of an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal
The inability to achieve satisfactory performance levels in competitive athletics

answer:
The correct answer is B. Disability is any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human being.

This is different from impairment (Q1), which is just lack of function. Disability is about the inability to achieve goals because of that lack of function — you can have an impairment, such as a minor limp, that results in no disability at all.

stem: _______ cells are responsible for building bone while ________ cells are responsible for reabsorbing bone. These two cells are referred to collectively as the ______________.
answer:
The correct answer is A. Osteoblasts (bone building) + osteoclasts (bone resorbing) = the basic multicellular unit.

Osteoblast vs. osteocyte — the key's own note, worth keeping: osteoblasts produce the non-cellular bone structure (collagen and matrix proteins) and are the major builders of bone tissue. Osteoblasts transform into osteocytes once they surround themselves with bone tissue, at which point the osteocytes maintain and slowly replace bone over time.

answer:
The correct answer is D. From middle to ends: diaphysis (middle portion) → metaphysis → growth plate → epiphysis. The epiphysis is covered in articular cartilage.

stem: In which of the following cases would you order a CT scan of the spine?

options.html: A 40-year-old woman with a 6 week history of what appears to be mechanical pain radiating to the buttocks, that has had only minimal improvement with consistent PT sessions.
A 20-year-old male with morning stiffness in the back that improves with activity, and back pain that worsens nightly.

A 70-year-old woman with back pain radiating down to her right leg and toes for 3 months, despite consistent PT sessions and regular use of Acetaminophen. There is subjective weakness and numbness on the right lateral leg. No bladder, bowel or erectile dysfunction.
a 30-year-old man in a MVC this morning, has severe neck pain despite analgesics. X-rays of C-Spine were normal.

answer:
The correct answer is D. CT is the modality for an occult fracture after trauma with negative plain films — that is the whole point of the question. Each distractor is a different modality:

  • A — this patient may simply benefit from further PT. If PT has been sufficient, the next step is x-ray (more accessible, less radiation) or MRI if suspecting spinal stenosis.
  • B — this is inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness improving with activity, worse at night), which requires MRI if imaging is indicated.
  • C — needs MRI after a long course of therapy, with a presentation consistent with nerve root compression.

stem: A 25 y/o olympian gymnast came in after an injury at practice, he had sustained a fall and landed on his back. X-ray showed a fracture in her vertebrae at the thoracic level there are no evidence of any lateral shift or fracture, which type of deformity might he present later?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A vertebral fracture can cause the spine to come closer together, giving a "hump" appearance — and that is especially true at the thoracic level, which is where kyphosis lives.

The distractors are excluded by location or cause: lordosis is lower, at the lumbar section; malformation is usually congenital; scoliosis is a lateral deformity, and the stem explicitly says there is no lateral shift.

stem: You see a patient in your family clinic who complains of lower back pain. What red flags findings are you looking for on history and physical exam? (Choose 5 answers)
answer:
The correct answers are B, C, G, I, K. Red flags for lower back pain:

  • Night/rest pain ← B
  • Saddle anesthesia ← C
  • Weight loss ← G
  • Incontinence ← I
  • IV drug use ← K
  • advanced age (fragility fracture risk)
  • previous cancer history
  • immunosuppression (HIV, steroids)
  • trauma
  • erectile dysfunction

Note that saddle anesthesia and incontinence together are the cauda equina syndrome pair — the emergency this screen exists to catch.

stem: An elderly man comes to the emergency department complaining of shoulder pain after a fall. Upon physical exam you note decreased range of motion. When you lift his arm vertically above his head and then ask him to slowly lower it back down to his side you note that his arm is controlled at first and then drops abruptly to his side. What is the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. This is the Drop Arm test, a classic test for rotator cuff injury (the other is the empty can test). The arm falls because of a supraspinatus tear.

C is excluded by the manoeuvre itself: with a shoulder dislocation you would not be able to lift the man's arm completely above his head in the first place. See rotator cuff tendinopathy and rotator cuff muscles.

stem: Which ligaments are damaged during a separated or sprung shoulder?
answer:
The correct answer is B. In a typical shoulder separation, the ligaments that may be damaged are the acromioclavicular, the coracoclavicular (trapezoid and conoid) and/or the coracoacromial.

The discriminator across the options is the coracohumeral ligament, which appears in A, C, D and E and is not part of the injury — the trapezoid and conoid are the coracoclavicular ligament, which is what makes B complete.

stem: What is it called when there is partial but incomplete separation of joints in the shoulder where joint articulating surfaces are misaligned?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The three real terms, all defined against each other:

  • Apprehension — the fear that the shoulder will subluxate or dislocate, which may prevent full participation in work or sport
  • Subluxation — partial but incomplete dislocation; articulating surfaces misaligned
  • Dislocation — complete separation of the joint's articulating surfaces

"Demi-dislocation" is not a term. See glenohumeral joint.

stem: Ms. S, a 25-year-old female, sees you in your family clinic for right arm pain that has been bothering her for 2 months. Which of the following symptoms would lead you to believe that she has neuropathic pain? (Choose 5 answers)
answer:
The correct answers are A, E, H, I, J. Symptoms of neuropathic pain:

  • Shooting pain ← A
  • Tingling/numbness ← E (also known as paresthesias)
  • Burning pain ← H
  • Hyperalgesia ← I — pain beyond expectation in response to a normally painful stimulus
  • Allodynia ← J — pain in response to a normally non-painful stimulus

Note that F (diminished sensation) and G (analgesia) are negative sensory phenomena — they can accompany nerve injury but are not the pain symptoms the question asks for. B and C are nociceptive descriptors (compare Q11).

flags.title: No answer in the workbook — and the question is ambiguous
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83, so Q85 is unanswered, and unlike Q84 there is no other passage in the workbook that settles it.

The likely intended answer is D, the ulnar nerve, on the reasoning that the lower plexus (C8-T1) is the ulnar nerve's origin and lower-plexus/Klumpke-type injuries are what Q64 has just covered. However, brachial plexus injury patterns depend entirely on mechanism — upper plexus (Erb-Duchenne, Q61) injuries are the more common obstetric and traction pattern, which would favour the axillary or musculocutaneous nerve — so the "most commonly affected" framing has no single defensible answer as written. Verify against a real source; do not memorize a letter here.

stem: A 25-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with numbness and tingling in her right arm and hand. She reports that the symptoms are worse at night and interfere with her sleep. On examination, you note weakness in the muscles innervated by the median nerve, including the flexor pollicis longus, the flexor digitorum profundus, and the pronator teres. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
answer: The answer is C — the median nerve.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook, and the stem gives itself away
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83, so Q86 is unanswered. C is unambiguous only because the stem itself names the median nerve ("weakness in the muscles innervated by the median nerve") before asking which nerve is affected.

The clinically interesting point the question fails to ask: the muscles listed — flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus and pronator teres — are proximal median-innervated muscles that lie above the carpal tunnel. Weakness in them therefore points to a proximal median neuropathy (pronator teres syndrome / anterior interosseous involvement), not carpal tunnel syndrome — even though the "worse at night, interferes with sleep" history is written to sound like carpal tunnel.

stem: A patient comes to you following a soccer game where a soccer ball was kicked up striking the end of their index finger head on. On examination the finger is swollen and they have lost the ability to keep the DIP in an extended position. Function of the rest of the finger, while hindered by swelling, appears to be normal. What is this injury called and how do you manage it?

options.html: Boutonnière deformity and it is managed with surgery
Mallet finger and it is managed with radiologic imaging and splinting in an extended position
Jersey finger and it is managed with radiologic imaging, grip and finger extension exercises
Trigger finger and it is a self-limiting condition

answer:
The correct answer is B. mallet finger — loss of DIP extension after a direct blow to the fingertip. Management is continuous extension for 6-8 weeks. Surgery has been used but is often not necessary; it becomes an option for patients whose injury becomes chronic and fails splinting.

Contrast the named deformities: Boutonnière is loss of PIP extension; Jersey finger is loss of DIP flexion (FDP avulsion); trigger finger is catching on flexion (see Q38).

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to you with complaints of his 3rd and 4th digits clicking when he flexes and extends his fingers. He is currently limiting his flexion in order to avoid reaching the point where the clicking occurs because he has had incidents where his fingers lock and it is very painful to unlock them. This has resulted in him not being able to manage his duties at work as a manual labourer. What is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Splint in extension for two weeks
Inject steroids into the area to try and relieve pain/swelling

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is trigger finger, and the question is really about where on the escalation ladder this patient sits:

  • B (nothing) is reasonable when it is not painful, the patient is not pushing for therapy, and function is unaffected — but his work is affected.
  • C (steroid injection) is reasonable because he wants further treatment and his function is impaired.
  • D (surgery) — surgical release of the flexor tendon sheath — is for patients who have failed a trial of steroid injection and remain impaired.

stem: A patient has pain during walking in their weight bearing leg. The pain is localized to the anterior groin region, as the leg goes into extension. You place the patient in a supine position and examine their muscular function and range of motion. Your findings are relatively normal except pain on hip flexion and passive hip extension near the end range of motion. Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: The most likely muscle group involved are the hamstrings
This is referred to as a Trendelenburg gait and is a result of gluteus medius injury/weakness
This is likely referred pain from sciatic nerve impingement
This could be a result of muscle, tendon sheath, or bursitis pain associated with the iliopsoas muscle

answer:
The correct answer is D. The iliopsoas and its associated structures are the likely cause, because both active recruitment (hip flexion) and passive stretching (hip extension) of the psoas reproduce the pain — that pattern is the diagnosis.

A and C are wrong on location: that pain would be in the posterior buttock and down the thigh, not the anterior groin. B is wrong on gait: a Trendelenburg pattern with pelvic instability is not what the case describes.

stem: Which muscle group and innervation is not correctly matched:

options.html: Quadriceps muscles supplied by the femoral nerve
Adductor longus, brevis and magnus supplied by the obturator nerve, except the hamstring portion of magnus which is the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve
Gluteus maximus supplied by the superior gluteal nerve and the gluteus medius and minimus supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve

Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of the biceps femoris supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic and the short head of the biceps femoris supplied by the fibular division of the sciatic

answer:
The correct answer is C — it has the two gluteal nerves swapped. Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve; gluteus medius and minimus by the superior gluteal nerve.

How to remember it: picture the muscles in anatomical position — medius and minimus are the more superior muscles, and conveniently they take the superior gluteal nerve. See femoral nerve, obturator nerve, sciatic nerve.

stem: Identify the ligament that is incorrectly matched to its function in stabilizing the knee.

options.html: Medial collateral ligament – resist valgus force on the knee
Fibular collateral ligament – resist varus forces on the knee
Anterior cruciate ligament – resist posterior translation of the femur on the tibial plateau
Posterior cruciate ligament – resist anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur

answer:
The correct answer is D. The PCL does not resist anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur — that is the ACL's job.

Reason it from the exam manoeuvre: think of the posterior sag sign or the translation of the tibia during the posterior drawer test (which tests for PCL rupture), and you can see the PCL resists POSTERIOR translation of the tibia relative to the femur. See anterior cruciate ligament.

stem: A rugby player plants his foot forward before being wrapped up and tackled from the right. The result is a valgus force on the knee in a flexed position with some external rotation of the lower leg. What structures are commonly injured in this type of trauma?

options.html: The fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus
The quadriceps tendon and the IT band
The anterior cruciate ligament, medial meniscus and the Medial collateral ligament
The medial meniscus, posterior cruciate ligament, the hamstrings muscles

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is the Unhappy Triad: ACL + medial meniscus + MCL. Trace the mechanism:

  • The valgus force overcomes the MCL → MCL injury
  • Because the MCL attaches to the medial meniscus, an MCL tear of this nature drags a medial meniscal tear with it
  • The ACL is injured by the combination of external rotation of the tibia while the knee is semi-flexed

The key's own comment: "This is guaranteed to be on your test."

stem: Which of the following regarding meniscal injury is true?

options.html: Lateral meniscal tears should be suspected with injury of the fibular collateral ligament because it is fused to the lateral meniscus
Tears of the more central meniscus are faster to heal because they receive blood supply from the geniculate vessels
The peripheral portion of the meniscus receives better blood supply from the capsular vessels than the central portion
The lateral meniscus is often involved in what is referred to as the unhappy triad

answer:
The correct answer is C. The peripheral meniscus is better supplied by the capsular vessels — which is why peripheral tears heal the quickest.

  • B is backwards: central tears are nourished only by synovial fluid and are relatively slow to heal.
  • D is the wrong meniscus: it is the medial meniscus that features in the unhappy triad (Q26).
  • A is the wrong pair: the fibular collateral ligament and lateral meniscus are not connected — it is the medial pair (MCL and medial meniscus) that are fused.

See meniscus tear.

stem: A 25-year-old patient comes to your office complaining of pain on the lateral side of the knee. There is no history of trauma. He experiences it most during workouts such as squatting and lunges and when climbing the stairs to his apartment. On examination you find he has normal flexion and extension with no neurological findings. On palpation you find tenderness over the lateral side of the knee and fibular head. The knee is stable during the anterior/posterior drawer test as well as during varus and valgus stress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. iliotibial band inflammation — a young active patient with characteristic pain over the IT band insertion during loading such as squatting and stair climbing.

  • A — no anterior knee swelling or pain reported
  • B — no signs of patellar pathology, and the pain is not anterior (see patellofemoral pain syndrome)
  • C and D — no history of trauma, which you would expect for these injuries in a young person, and no instability (MCL) or catching/locking (meniscal)

stem: Which of these patients requires further assessment and an x-ray?

options.html: An 18-year-old female trips over a soccer ball while playing pick-up in a park. She is unable to weight bear on her left leg following the injury and is partially carried and driven to UH to see you. In the emergency department she still cannot weight bear to let you see her gait.
A 26-year-old male comes in limping from a construction site. He can slightly weight bear during his limping. On examination you note tenderness in the last 4 cm of lateral malleolus.
A 45-year-female comes in after tripping while getting out of the shower. On examination she has marked tenderness over the base of the 5th metatarsal.
All of the patients above need an ankle or foot X-ray series

answer:
The correct answer is D. Apply the Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules:

  • Ankle series if unable to weight bear immediately post-trauma AND in the emergency room → patient A
  • Ankle series if pain over the bottom 6 cm of the medial OR lateral malleolus → patient B (4 cm falls inside 6 cm)
  • Foot series if pain over the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular bone → patient C

stem: A patient comes to you after rolling her ankle. You note that she is not able to weight bear and so you send her for an x-ray. Which of the following are incorrect management?

options.html: You should image the ankle properly with an AP, lateral and mortise view
You find that the patient has an ankle with an approximate displacement of her medial malleolus by 1 mm, with the mortise undisplaced. You decide to manage her with conservative treatment

You find that the patient has an ankle with bi-malleolar fracture, but the mortise is not displaced, and the medial malleolus displaced under 2 mm. This patient should be considered for surgical management.
Ankle fractures classified as B and C are regarded as 'unstable'
All of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is E — all of the above are true.

  • A — AP, lateral and mortise are the normal ankle series.
  • B — the findings meet the criteria for non-operative treatment: (i) single malleolus involvement, (ii) mortise undisplaced, (iii) <2 mm of malleolar displacement.
  • C — correctly escalates, because it involves a bimalleolar fracture (failing criterion i).
  • D — Weber categories: A = fracture below the syndesmosis, B = fracture at the syndesmosis, C = fracture above the malleolus. With fractures below the syndesmosis and only 1 malleolus involved, the ankle is relatively stable and can likely be managed conservatively — so B and C are the unstable ones.

stem: A patient comes to you following a long run in the woods. They complain of having stepped into a pot hole and having their right foot forcefully pushed up toward their shin (dorsiflexed) and hearing a 'pop'. Following she had a great deal of pain. On examination you note a swollen painful ankle with a concentration of swelling on the back of the ankle and heel. On examination you find she has 5- strength in dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion, and a 1 in plantar flexion. What statement is correct?

options.html: The patient appears to have sustained a L4-5 injury, and is likely to display what is called a 'drop foot'.
The patient likely has a likely ankle sprain. The side whether talofibular ligaments or deltoid ligaments have not yet been determined by this examination.
Patient seems to be suffering from a common runner's injury called 'plantar fasciitis'
This patient would be expected to have a positive Thompson test, and may have a history of gout and seronegative arthropathies.

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is an Achilles tendon rupture — suspected from the isolated loss of plantar flexor strength (grade 1), the characteristic swelling at the back of the heel, and the history of forceful dorsiflexion. A positive Thompson test confirms it. There is also an association with chronic tendonitis seen in patients with gout and seronegative arthropathies, though that history is not required.

  • B is possible with this mechanism, but the specific loss of plantar flexor tone, the location of swelling, and no pain over the medial or lateral ankle argue against a simple ankle sprain.
  • C — plantar fasciitis was possibly present in a runner, but would not produce this swelling or loss of plantar flexor strength.

See Achilles tendinopathy.

stem: Neuropathic pain is:

options.html: Pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease
Pain caused from stretching of visceral tissues resulting in poorly localized cramping pain
Pain resulting from local tissue damage that is well localized but with variable descriptions

answer:
The correct answer is A. Neuropathic pain is pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease.

The distractors are the two nociceptive subtypes:

  • B → visceral nociceptive pain (stretching of visceral tissue; poorly localized, cramping)
  • C → somatic nociceptive pain (local tissue damage; well localized, variable descriptors)

See 05 - Neuropathic Pain and Q65 for the symptom list.

stem: Wallerian degeneration is the process of _____ nerve tract degeneration _____ to the site of injury.
answer: The correct answer is D. Wallerian degeneration is the breakdown of nerve tissue that occurs when a nerve is transected through traumatic injury. Degeneration starts at the site of injury and progresses distally (anterograde), obliterating the nerve segment distal to the injury. See Q66 for where this fits among neuropraxia/axonotmesis/neurotmesis.

stem: Localize the following physical exam findings: The patient is stepping with their affected foot in a plantar flexed position during swing phase of normal gait and makes contact with their forefoot. The patient has MRC grade 3 strength in dorsiflexion and 4+ in plantar flexion.

Temporary loss of sensory and motor function from transient neural ischemia & edema. Patients usually make a full recovery

stem: A 73-year-old patient comes to you with a several year history of bilateral knee pain that is worse on the right side. On examination you find MRC 5 for knee extension and flexion as well as a normal neurologic examination. On palpation you see his knees are slightly swollen but not red or hot. You find there is joint line tenderness and crepitus with passive movement. There is no sign of patellar apprehension or grinding. Anterior and posterior drawer tests are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Central medial meniscal tear from twisting

answer:
The correct answer is D. Arthritis — the patient's age 73 (over 50), the long history without trauma, crepitus on movement and joint line tenderness all point there.

B is the most likely meniscal injury for an elderly patient, but there is no history of trauma and no evidence of true locking. C is unlikely with no grinding or patellar apprehension on exam.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A patient comes to you with an antalgic gait and some swelling over the great toe of the left foot. She had become upset during a personal matter and kicked her door. Upon examination you find that the toe is extremely painful for the patient and you decide to get an x-ray. You see a transverse fracture of the distal phalange of the great toe with no involvement of articular surface. How do you manage?

options.html: Do nothing, toe injuries generally require no treatment
Buddy tape the great toe to the next toe
Activity modification, physio and no weight bearing

answer:
The correct answer is B. Buddy taping is appropriate when there is no displacement and no involvement of the articular surface. Note the two escalation triggers embedded in that rule:

  • displacement → surgery
  • articular surface involvement → foot and toe cast

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 16 y.o. F. pianist came in with progressive swollen joints (multiple) over the last three months, more than 6 joints involved in her hands, they feel warm and tender on palpation, what are your top 3 differential diagnoses?
answer:
The correct answers are B, E, F. The patient demographic (female, late teen) fits RA, SLE and JIA best. The condition is chronic (over three months) with multiple joints involved.

Each exclusion turns on one feature:

  • A Infectious — ruled out by the chronic, polyarticular course
  • C AS — more likely in the lower back
  • D Acute gout — usually one joint, and this is a chronic patient
  • G Chondrosarcoma — a large mass around bigger joints, not a polyarthritis

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[04 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[06 - Osteoarthritis]], [[07 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[08 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 50-year-old female patient comes to you complaining of aching in her knees and feet that has been occurring daily, she has minor pains in the morning but the pain progresses with activity throughout the day especially with walking. In history you get the impression that this pain is bothersome but is not limiting her function. On exam you notice slight bowing (varus deformity) in her knees. Overall outside the pain, the patient does not complain of fever, nausea, or fatigue. You order a radiograph to assess her knees and ankles, what do you expect?

options.html: Subchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes, eccentric cartilage loss, loose bodies
Osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling

answer:
The correct answer is A. We suspect osteoarthritis because of the daily pain that progresses through the day and worsens with activity, supported by the absence of systemic symptoms (fever, fatigue, nausea) that would point toward rheumatoid arthritis.

Note that B and C are the RA radiographic picture — osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling and symmetric joint space narrowing — whereas OA gives eccentric cartilage loss with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: Repetitive strain injuries (RSI) are caused by maximal or over the maximal exertion
Around 5% of the Canadian General population experience chronic pain
Opioid analgesics can result in Respiratory depression, mental clouding, nausea/vomiting, constipation, drug tolerance
The majority of the chronic pain are caused through the nociceptive pathway whereas the acute pain are usually neuropathic

answer:
The correct answer is C. All of those are side effects of opioids. Each other option has a specific error:

  • A — RSI is caused by submaximal exertion over a period of time without recovery (sitting in a funny position for too long), not maximal exertion.
  • B — around 30%, not 5%, of the Canadian general population experience chronic pain.
  • D — backwards: chronic pain is more neuropathic, acute pain more nociceptive.

See 01 - Understanding and Managing Chronic Pain.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: What is the dose referred to as the 'watchful dose' in opioid management?
answer:
The correct answer is D. 90 mg/day of morphine or equivalent is the "watchful dose" — where significant increases in side effects such as constipation appear, and where the risk of drug diversion/sale rises.

To manage risk at this level, some suggest titrating opioids for a 30% increase in function or reduction in pain.

C is the old answer: in previous years 200 mg was the watchful dose; the updated guidelines moved it to 90 mg.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following is false about ASA?

options.html: Indication: pain, fever, anti-inflammatory in high doses, anti-thrombotic in low dose
Contraindications include hypersensitivity reactions to NSAIDs and children with fever (risks of Reyes syndrome)
Adverse drug reaction includes GI bleeding, tinnitus in high doses, hypersensitivities, prolonged bleeding
Aspirin has little to no toxicity and mortality risk

answer:
The correct answer is D. There is significant risk of overdose with aspirin, due to rapid saturation of the drug's conjugation system — once conjugation saturates, kinetics shift and levels climb disproportionately.

A-C are all accurate: dose-dependent indications, contraindication in children with fever because of Reye syndrome, and the ADR profile including tinnitus at high doses.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Arthritis & Pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[11 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following does not have anti-inflammatory effects?
answer: The correct answer is B. Acetaminophen has antipyretic and analgesic effects but essentially no anti-inflammatory effects — which is exactly what separates it from the NSAIDs. All the other listed drugs do have anti-inflammatory effects.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A comminuted fracture is a:

options.html: Fracture involving the flare of a long bone
Fracture involving more than two fragments

answer:
The correct answer is D. Comminuted = more than two fragments. The distractors are the other descriptors:

  • A → diaphyseal fracture
  • B → metaphyseal fracture ("the flare")
  • C → intra-articular fracture

stem: Complete the following statement: A _____ fracture does not involve external environmental contamination and has _____ outcomes whereas a _____ fracture involves contamination of soft tissues and has _____ outcomes.
answer: The correct answer is B. Closed → better; open → poorer.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A greenstick fracture is a:

options.html: Fracture involving the epiphysis and intra-articular surface
Pediatric fracture involving the growth plates and results in poorer bone development
Pediatric fracture that occurs because young bone is softer and less brittle

answer: The correct answer is D. A greenstick fracture is a pediatric fracture occurring because young bone is softer and less brittle — it bends and cracks on one side rather than snapping through. See Q82, where the radiographic appearance is the question.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A unique complication of fractures involving growth plates is:
answer: The correct answer is C. Growth arrest. Note the word unique in the stem: infection and non-union (A, B) are common complications of any fracture, so neither is unique to physeal injury. Excess ossification (D) is not a fracture complication. See Salter-Harris fractures.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: Which of the following is a typical reason why casting may fail to maintain reduction?

options.html: padding doesn't affect success of reduction

answer: The correct answer is A. Excess padding interferes with proper reduction — the limb can move inside the cast, so the cast no longer holds the alignment.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: You are counselling Mr. M about potential complications following surgical treatment of his fractured tibia. Which of the following are potential complications that you should discuss with him?

options.html: Non-union: failure of a fracture to heal after adequate realignment often due to poor blood supply
Avascular necrosis: degeneration of a piece of bone due to inadequate blood supply
Arthritis: can result from malunion or joint space narrowing resulting in degeneration of articular surfaces.

answer: The correct answer is E. Non-union, avascular necrosis and arthritis are all possible complications after fracture of a bone — and each definition as given in the options is correct.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: What are the six stages of fracture healing in their appropriate order?

options.html: Inflammatory stage, hard callus stage, remodelling stage, hematoma stage, granulation stage, soft callus stage
Hematoma stage, inflammatory stage, granulation stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, remodelling stage
Inflammatory stage, hematoma stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, granulation stage, remodelling stage
Hematoma stage, inflammatory stage, granulation stage, remodelling stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage
Remodeling stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, inflammatory stage, hematoma stage, granulation stage

answer: The correct answer is B. Hematoma → inflammatory → granulation → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The two ordering rules that eliminate every distractor: hematoma comes first (bleeding precedes the inflammatory response) and remodelling comes last.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling off his skateboard onto his outstretched right hand. He reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move his hand. On physical exam, there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomical snuffbox and decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. FOOSH injuries are a common cause of wrist fractures, with the scaphoid the most commonly fractured bone in the wrist. The anatomical snuffbox is on the radial side of the wrist and contains the scaphoid; snuffbox tenderness is the classic finding, and patients may also have decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand from injury to the superficial radial nerve.

The distractors, each with its own signature:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius with dorsal displacement, typically older patients with osteoporosis (see Q84)
  • Radial head fracture — at the elbow; adults who FOOSH with an extended elbow
  • Distal radius fracture — common, but does not involve the anatomical snuffbox

See scaphoid fracture.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on her outstretched hand. She reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move her hand. X-rays are negative for fracture, but there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomic snuffbox and the patient is unable to grip objects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Place the wrist in a cast for 6 weeks
Perform a CT scan of the wrist
Order an MRI of the wrist

answer:
The correct answer is D. A negative x-ray does not rule out a scaphoid fracture — scaphoid fractures may not be visible on initial films. With high clinical suspicion, order an MRI, which is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing them.

Why the rest fail: A — casting for 6 weeks without proper diagnosis may lead to further complications. B — a repeat x-ray in 1 week may still not show the fracture. C — CT shows better detail than plain film, but MRI is the modality of choice.

Why this matters: a scaphoid fracture is a serious injury and can lead to avascular necrosis of the bone if left untreated — the same blood-supply logic as Q13.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off his bike and injuring his forearm. X-rays reveal an incomplete fracture of the radius with evidence of cortical thickening on the convex side of the bone, and no significant displacement or angulation. Which of the following types of fractures is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Incomplete fracture with cortical thickening on the convex side is characteristic of a greenstick fracture. These are common in children because of the pliability of their bones, and typically occur in long bones when a bending force is applied.

The distractors:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius fracture in older adults who FOOSH
  • Monteggia fracture — fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head
  • Buckle fracture — an incomplete fracture with bulging of the cortex on one side due to compression
  • Torus fracture — another term for a buckle fracture, which is why C and D cannot both be the single best answer

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of falling onto his outstretched arm during a football game. He complains of severe pain in his left shoulder and inability to move it. On examination, his left arm is held in adduction and internal rotation. X-ray reveals a dislocated humeral head posterior to the glenoid. What is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Trauma is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations, accounting for approximately 75-90% of cases.

Seizures and electric shock can also cause posterior dislocations — they are the classically taught associations — but they are much less common, which is the trap this question sets. A rotator cuff tear is not a cause of posterior dislocation.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[05 - Fracture Radiology]], [[07 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department after falling on her outstretched hand. She complains of wrist pain and deformity. On examination, her wrist is swollen and tender, and there is an obvious dorsal angulation of the distal radius. X-ray reveals a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement. What is the name of this fracture?
answer: The answer is D — Colles fracture.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83; there is no entry for Q84. The answer above is reasoned, but it is well supported by the workbook's own text elsewhere: Q78's explanation defines a Colles fracture as "a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the wrist... typically seen in older patients with osteoporosis" — exactly this stem.

The distractors: Smith fracture is the reverse (distal radius with volar/palmar displacement); Monteggia is proximal ulna + radial head dislocation (per Q82); Barton is an intra-articular distal radius fracture with carpal subluxation.

lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Exaggerated lateral curvature of the spine is:
answer:
The correct answer is C. Scoliosis is the lateral curvature.

  • Lordosis — increased anterior curvature; either excessive lumbar curvature or reduced cervical curvature
  • Kyphosis — increased posterior curvature, normally used of exaggerated thoracic curvature
  • "Lateral curveosis" is not a real term.

stem: What are the Red Flags of abnormal gait in a child? (Select all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are B, C, D, E. A and F are wrong because they are the reassuring versions of two red flags — it is asymmetry and a suspected related condition that are the red flags, not symmetry and the absence of one.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following are involved in the 'Ponsetti treatment'?

options.html: Weekly manipulations with casting to correct varus foot deformities
Achilles tendon lengthening to correct equinus ankle positioning
This is treatment for cases of talipes equinovarus

answer: The correct answer is E. Options A-C describe the steps of the Ponseti treatment, and D correctly names the condition — talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).

weekLabel: Week 11 - Fractures, Rheumatology Treatment & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following about the natural history and etiology of club foot is correct?

options.html: The natural history includes progressive worsening of deformity and stiffness with gradual loss of ambulation
The etiology like calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus is related to intrauterine positioning rather than genetics
This condition appears to be more prevalent among females
All of the above are correct

answer:
The correct answer is A. That is the correct description of the natural history of congenital talipes equinovarus.

B is the substantive error: there are many etiological theories for clubfoot — arrested embryologic development, neurologic causes, muscular fibrosis — and there is some relationship with polygenic multifactorial inheritance, so it cannot be attributed to intrauterine positioning alone the way calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus can.

lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: In the analysis and description of curvature in a scoliosis patient requires the following except:

options.html: Ruling out any anatomical abnormalities (i.e. from trauma or tumours)
All of the above are required

answer:
The correct answer is F — all of the above are required. What each term means when describing a scoliosis curve:

  • Location — whether the vertex of the curve is cervical, thoracic or lumbar
  • Spinal level — the actual levels the curvature spans
  • Direction — whether the concavity points right or left
  • Magnitude — the number of degrees
  • Abnormalities — is there a fracture cause or tumour driving the curvature that could be addressed

lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following are not a risk factor for further progression of scoliosis.

options.html: Onset at an older physiologic age
Thoracic are at greater risk than lumbar
Larger curves are at greater risk than smaller curves

answer: The correct answer is A. Patients who are physiologically older have less skeletal bone growth remaining, and therefore less potential for progression of scoliosis through asymmetric bone growth. Progression risk tracks remaining growth — so younger onset is the risk, not older.

stem: A 16-year-old patient comes to you with complaints of a rib hump that was noticed during a physiotherapy session for a shoulder injury she had. You complete a neurological examination which is normal as well as characterize her spinal curvature. You note a Right Thoracic curve from level T7-T12 with a 34-degree curve. The most appropriate treatment would be:

options.html: Follow the person with annual radiologic examination to assess progression

answer: The correct answer is C. Bracing. Patients with 30-40 degrees of curve are recommended to have bracing treatment, with the main goal of preventing further progression (not of correcting the existing curve). Her 34° falls squarely in that band. See scoliosis.

stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with hip pain and an abnormal gait. Imaging reveals a femoral head displacement, which was not initially evident on plain radiographs. The patient has a BMI of 35, and is undergoing hormonal therapy for a pre-existing medical condition. Which of the following management options is most appropriate for this patient?

options.html: Observation and follow-up imaging in 4 weeks
Non-weight bearing with crutches and physical therapy
Surgical reduction and internal fixation of the hip
Encourage weight loss and activity modification

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is SCFE, and the stem's two risk factors — high BMI and hormonal therapy — are what flag it.

Surgical reduction and internal fixation is typically required for moderate to severe cases, to prevent further displacement and degenerative arthritis. B may be appropriate for some cases, and A for mild ones — but the pain and abnormal gait here suggest a moderate to severe case. D is beneficial for overall health and future prevention but is not sufficient treatment for an acute SCFE.

lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[04 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: A 4-year-old girl presents to the clinic with a history of frequent falls and difficulty with balance. She also complains of leg pain at night that is relieved by rubbing. On physical exam, she has a waddling gait and is unable to stand on one leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD) is a non-traumatic condition of the hip joint in children, occurring when blood flow to the femoral head is interrupted, leading to bone death and subsequent deformation.

Symptoms: hip or groin pain, limping, difficulty with mobility. Nighttime pain relieved by rubbing is a classic feature. Children may have a waddling gait and be unable to stand on one leg.

DDH, JIA, osteogenesis imperfecta and SCFE can present similarly — the history and exam here are what favour LCPD. Note the age contrast with Q80: LCPD in a 4-year-old, SCFE in a 13-year-old.

options.html: Failure to relieve pain or confirm diagnosis

answer: The correct answer is G — all of the above. All of these are possible. The consent principle: communicate risks that are frequent as well as those that are very serious — include everything any reasonable person would want to know. See bursitis and corticosteroids.

You are now assessing if there are any contraindications to administering this treatment to the patient. What from this list is a contraindication/relative contraindication to administering the injection?

options.html: Infection on the skin over the trochanter
Inability to properly position the patient

answer: The correct answer is F — all of the above. In addition to those four, you must confirm that you have the patient's consent, the ability to manage an emergency situation, and adequate equipment, assistance and monitoring. See trochanteric bursitis.

stem: Why is it important to have multiple Xray views when assessing a fracture? (select all that apply)

options.html: To pick up microfractures that may only be seen in one view
To differentiate between a transverse and linear fracture
To assess whether an oblique fracture is actually a spiral fracture
To check whether tendons are involved in an avulsion fracture

answer: The correct answer is A, C, E. some microfractures may only be seen in one view. A transverse and linear fracture are very different, and can be differentiated from a single view. A spiral fracture may look like an oblique fracture in one view, so it is important to obtain another view to differentiate the two. Tendons cannot be seen well on Xrays. Rotational fractures usually need two views to look at joints proximally and distally to interpret the degree and type of rotation.

stem: Tobiloba is a 19 year old woman coming to see you in the family medicine clinic with gradually worsening bilateral anterior knee pain. She describes the pain as deep and aching. She first noticed the pain when she increased her hurdles training volume, and initially the pain was brought on by exercise. However, the pain is now brought on when she climbs stairs and stands up after prolonged periods of sitting. Based on the most likely diagnosis, what would you offer Tobiloba? Choose all that are correct.
answer: The correct answer is A, C, D, E. Given the presentation and the demographics of this case, Tobiloba most likely has patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Because PFPS is related to increased Q angle, physiotherapy may focus on quadriceps strengthening (especially vastus medialis) to prevent lateral translation of the patella during knee flexion. stem: A 63 y.o Finnish patient presents to the ER with sudden painless vision loss, an awful headache, pain with chewing, and pain with laying his head on their pillow at night. options.html: Consult oncology urgently due to risk of intracranial malignancy
Consult ophthalmology for a temporal artery biopsy

answer: The correct answer is A, E, F. This patient has giant cell arteritis. Low-dose prednisone is only reserved for cases where other options don’t work or there are difficulty discontinuing steroids. Medium-dose prednisone is for RA flares, polymyalgia rheumatica and acute gout flare. Remember to not wait for ESR/CRP results and to start high dose corticosteroids immediately! stem: A 58-year-old woman has deep aching shoulder pain. Active range of motion is reduced but passive range is full, and rotator cuff strength is poor. X-ray shows symmetric joint space loss, erosions and osteopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. Passive ROM separates the two: inflammatory arthritis loses active but not passive motion and has weak cuff muscles, with symmetric joint space, erosions and osteopenia on x-ray (reverse arthroplasty if surgery). Plantar fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis: plantar heel pain worse when initiating walking (first steps in the morning) plus point tenderness at the origin of the plantar fascia on the medial calcaneal tuberosity, often with a tight Achilles. Achilles tendinopathy hurts at the posterior heel near its insertion.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has had a foot ulcer for several months. It is now infected, with erythema and purulence but no systemic features. Because the ulcer is chronic, the infection is likely polymicrobial. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
answer: The correct answer is E. A wound alone does not mean infection. Mild, monomicrobial infections (S. aureus, S. pyogenes) can be treated with cefazolin; chronic ulcers are more likely polymicrobial (including gram-negatives) and need amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pip-tazo is for Pseudomonas. Start imaging with x-ray, then MRI for osteomyelitis; debridement is often needed.

stem: A 25-year-old man wakes with a wrist drop after falling asleep with his arm hooked over a chair. The nerve was compressed but not cut. Which type of injury is this and what is the expected course?
answer: The correct answer is A. Compression that damages myelin with the axon intact is neurapraxia: slowed conduction, temporary, typically resolving in 6-12 weeks (radial nerve "Saturday night" palsy). Axonotmesis (crush/stretch) loses the axon, which regrows about 1 inch per month. Neurotmesis (cut) disrupts the epineurium and cannot recover without surgery.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a hot, red, swollen knee and a fever. Aspiration shows cloudy fluid with gram-positive cocci in clusters. He has no MRSA risk factors. Along with blood cultures, what is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Oral cephalexin and repeat aspiration in a week
IV cefazolin plus irrigation and debridement
IV antibiotics alone without joint drainage

answer: The correct answer is B. Septic arthritis is an emergency: aspirate for the 3 Cs (cell count, culture/gram stain, crystals) and call ortho. Usual source is hematogenous seeding with S. aureus or streptococci. Treat with cefazolin (Ancef) 2 g IV q8h plus irrigation and debridement; vancomycin + ceftriaxone if MRSA risk.

stem: A 52-year-old man has an exquisitely painful, red first MTP joint that started overnight after a weekend of heavy drinking. Aspiration shows urate crystals. His serum uric acid today is normal. What should be done about the uric acid level?

options.html: Nothing more; a normal level excludes gout
Start allopurinol today to lower it
Repeat it once the attack has settled
Repeat it daily until it rises

answer: The correct answer is C. Serum uric acid can be normal during an acute gout attack, so check it during and again after the attack. The diagnosis rests on urate crystals in joint fluid. Triggers follow SMARTS (surgery, mechanical injury, alcohol, recent illness, travel, starting or stopping allopurinol); allopurinol prevents recurrence but is not started for the acute attack.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis develops an acutely swollen, warm knee over a day and a low-grade fever. Aspiration shows rhomboid-shaped crystals and a negative gram stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Pseudogout (CPPD) is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, typically in older patients with OA, most often the knee. It is less intense than gout but lasts longer, and can cause fever, so it must be separated from sepsis by aspiration. Rhomboid crystals = CPPD; needle-shaped crystals = gout. Treat like gout (indomethacin, IA or oral steroid).

stem: A 34-year-old daycare worker develops symmetric pain and swelling of the small joints of both hands a week after a febrile illness. Her CBC shows a new anemia. Which infection is most likely?
answer: The correct answer is A. Viral arthritis tends to be polyarticular, while bacterial arthritis is usually monoarticular. For an infectious polyarthritis think of endocarditis and viruses: parvovirus B19 (associated with anemia), hepatitis B/C and HIV. Gonococcal, Lyme and TB arthritis classically cause a large-joint monoarthritis.

stem: A 40-year-old man has swelling of several DIP joints, one whole "sausage" toe, and pitting of his fingernails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. DIP involvement points to psoriatic arthritis or OA; RA and the other CTDs usually spare the DIPs. Psoriatic arthritis adds dactylitis, enthesitis and nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) and is a clinical diagnosis. RA is symmetric small-joint arthritis of the hands and feet with more than an hour of morning stiffness.

stem: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night, with over an hour of morning stiffness that improves with exercise. Last year he had anterior uveitis. Chest expansion is reduced. Which investigation is most useful next?
answer: The correct answer is C. Inflammatory back pain (better with movement, second-half-of-night pain, long morning stiffness) with anterior uveitis and reduced chest expansion suggests ankylosing spondylitis. answer: The correct answer is D. stem: A 55-year-old woman has Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin of the fingers, telangiectasias, calcium deposits in the fingertips and heartburn from esophageal dysmotility. Which antibody is most associated with this presentation?
answer: The correct answer is A. This is CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia), the limited form of systemic sclerosis, associated with anti-centromere antibodies. Almost all SSc is ANA positive; anti-Scl-70 goes with diffuse disease and pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has 2 months of difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms. She has a violaceous rash on her upper eyelids and red papules over her knuckles. CK is markedly raised. Which association must be investigated?
answer: The correct answer is B. Inflammatory myositis causes proximal (shoulder and hip) weakness with raised CK. Dermatomyositis adds the heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and dilated nailfold capillaries, and in older adults it is associated with cancer, so screen for malignancy. Polymyositis has no rash or photosensitivity.

stem: A 45-year-old man feels a pop in the front of his elbow while lifting a heavy box. He has bruising, a bulge in the upper arm, and weak forearm supination. What is the most appropriate next step?
answer: The correct answer is C. Distal biceps rupture is rare, often acute with a pop, ecchymosis, a Popeye deformity and poor supination; rupture needs an orthopedic consult (the review calls it urgent). Proximal long-head ruptures are more common, degenerative and still functional, and are usually managed non-surgically.
